docs.text: Driver NTC thermistor driver ¶ A C++20 driver for any NTC thermistor read through a resistor divider into an ADC input: it turns a raw code into milli-degrees Celsius with integers only. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver knows no part. A thermistor is data : a table of resistance and temperature rows, Steinhart-Hart coefficients, or R25 and B for the beta equation, given in a Curve . The driver reads the divider node through a small port class you write, finds the thermistor's resistance, and looks the temperature up on the curve. Open and short circuits, a node outside the ADC's range and a part outside its rated window are errors with their own names, and every reading carries a bound. Temperature sensor, two terminals NTC thermistor Any maker: the part is data Measures : Temperature from the curve you declare, as milli-degrees Celsius Interface : A voltage divider into one ADC channel; optionally a GPIO that powers the divider only while it is read Arithmetic : Integers only: ohms, milli-degrees, millivolts, parts per million; no floating point, no library calls What you get ¶ Any NTC, no change of code. A part is a Curve ; the driver ships two presets and the way to write your own. See Presets and Configuration . Three ways to describe a part : a table of any 2 to 256 rows and any spacing, interpolated linearly in ln R, Steinhart-Hart coefficients, or R25 and B. tools/ntc_table.py makes a table from any of them or from a vendor's list. See Conversion . Faults by name : OpenCircuit , ShortCircuit , BelowRange , AboveRange , Unstable , CodeOutOfScale . See Troubleshooting . A bound on every reading from the tolerances you declare and one converter step. Tested without hardware against a model that shares no code with the driver. See Testing and CI . !!! warning "Not verified on hardware" The driver is host-tested against a model of the divider and fuzzed; it has not been run on a thermistor. The example preset (a TDK part) takes R25, B and the tolerances from the vendor's Rev.3 datasheet; its 39 table rows are a secondary listing, unverified because that sheet prints no table. Nothing generic depends on it. See Status and limitations . The object ¶ NtcThermistor<Port> holds a reference to your port and a Config . The constructor does no I/O and cannot fail. The object is not copyable or movable. Call Returns What it does EnsureInitialized() Result<void> Checks the configuration, brings the port's ADC up and switches the divider off. Returns Ok with no I/O once it has succeeded IsInitialized() bool Whether EnsureInitialized() has succeeded Read() Result<Reading> Samples, converts, returns the temperature, resistance, mean code and bound ReadResistance() Result<uint32_t> The same sampling, stopping at the divider arithmetic: ohms ReadRawCode() Result<uint32_t> One raw conversion in the same bias sequence, with no averaging and no maths: a diagnostic, no retry GetLastCode() uint32_t The last code the port returned, even one out of scale; no I/O SetConfig(config) Result<void> Replaces the configuration after validating it; the old one stays on failure GetConfig() const Config& The configuration in use Free functions, in inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp , with no port and no state: Function What it does Convert(config, code) The conversion of a code: the same maths as Read() ConvertResistance(config, code) The divider arithmetic only ToMilliKelvin(mc) , ToMilliFahrenheit(mc) Unit conversions, saturating SelfHeatingMicrowatts(config, r_ohm) The power the divider puts into the part Validate(config) The configuration check Read a temperature ¶ quickstart.cpp #include "ntc_thermistor.hpp" #include "ntc_thermistor_presets.hpp" // A 10 kOhm / B 3950 thermistor low-side in a 10 kOhm divider on a 12-bit ADC, // valid from -40 to +125 degC. constexpr ntc_thermistor :: Config kConfig {. curve = ntc_thermistor :: presets :: kGeneric10kB3950 , . min_temperature_mc = -40'000 , . max_temperature_mc = 125'000 }; int read_temperature_mc ( MyPort & port , int32_t & milli_celsius ) { ntc_thermistor :: NtcThermistor < MyPort > sensor ( port , kConfig ); // no I/O yet if ( auto r = sensor . EnsureInitialized (); ! r ) { // 1. check the config, bring the ADC up return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); // InvalidArgument or Bus } const auto t = sensor . Read (); // 2. sample, divider to ohms, curve to temperature if ( ! t ) { return static_cast < int > ( t . error ); // OpenCircuit, ShortCircuit, BelowRange, ... } milli_celsius = t . value . temperature_mc ; // 3. milli-degrees Celsius; // t.value.uncertainty_mc bounds it return 0 ; } Reading has temperature_mc (milli-degrees Celsius, window and offset applied), resistance_ohm , code (the mean) and uncertainty_mc (a bound on the declared tolerances). Use the maths alone ¶ api_tasks.cpp // The maths alone: a code the application already has, no port, no state. int32_t TemperatureOfCode ( uint32_t code ) { const auto r = ntc_thermistor :: Convert ( kConfig , code ); return r ? r . value . temperature_mc : INT32_MIN ; } Convert validates the configuration first, so the same call checks a Config and a code in a unit test of your own application. Handle every error ¶ api_tasks.cpp const char * Explain ( ntc_thermistor :: Error e ) { switch ( e ) { case ntc_thermistor :: Error :: OpenCircuit : return "no thermistor: cut wire, missing part, or a divider that is not " "powered" ; case ntc_thermistor :: Error :: ShortCircuit : return "node at the other rail: shorted part or wire, or the divider " "supply collapsed" ; case ntc_thermistor :: Error :: BelowRange : return "colder than the curve or the window" ; case ntc_thermistor :: Error :: AboveRange : return "hotter than the curve or the window" ; case ntc_thermistor :: Error :: Unstable : return "the samples disagree: a floating or noisy input" ; case ntc_thermistor :: Error :: CodeOutOfScale : return "the port returns more bits than Config::adc_bits says" ; default : break ; } return ntc_thermistor :: ToString ( e ); } Error Value When NotInitialized 1 A read before EnsureInitialized() succeeded InvalidArgument 2 The configuration is out of range or inconsistent (including a wait the port cannot make) Bus 3 ReadRaw() or SetBias() returned false OpenCircuit 16 The node is at the open rail: cut wire, missing part, divider not powered ShortCircuit 17 The node is at the short rail: shorted part or wire BelowRange 18 Colder than the curve or the window, or a resistance that does not fit 32 bits AboveRange 19 Hotter than the curve or the window, or a resistance of zero Unstable 20 The samples differ by more than max_spread_codes CodeOutOfScale 21 A sample is at or above 2^ adc_bits Timeout , DeviceIdMismatch , Crc , Busy , DeviceFault and Unsupported are never returned: a thermistor has no bus, no identity and no checksum. Trust a reading only as far as its bound ¶ api_tasks.cpp // The reading is a value and a bound: the true temperature lies within it if // the declared tolerances hold. bool WithinOneKelvin ( ntc_thermistor :: NtcThermistor < MyPort >& sensor , int32_t & temperature_mc ) { const auto t = sensor . Read (); if ( ! t || ( t . value . uncertainty_mc > 1000U )) { return false ; } temperature_mc = t . value . temperature_mc ; return true ; } Change the configuration at run time ¶ api_tasks.cpp // Change the offset at run time (a calibration): validated first, the old one // stays on failure. bool Calibrate ( ntc_thermistor :: NtcThermistor < MyPort >& sensor , int32_t offset_mc ) { ntc_thermistor :: Config c = sensor . GetConfig (); c . offset_mc = offset_mc ; return sensor . SetConfig ( c ). ok (); } Other units ¶ reference.cpp // Milli-kelvin and milli-fahrenheit, saturating; no floating point anywhere. int32_t ToFahrenheit ( int32_t milli_celsius ) { return ntc_thermistor :: ToMilliFahrenheit ( milli_celsius ); } Next: Configuration .

docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is built: the core, the free conversion functions, the port contract, and your port. The layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers. Drawn from: inc/ntc_thermistor.hpp public calls ; inc/ntc_thermistor_adc_interface.hpp AdcInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . Layer Files Owns Core inc/ntc_thermistor.hpp , src/ntc_thermistor.ipp Lifecycle, sampling, the bias sequence, the port hooks Conversion inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp The pure maths: classification, divider, curve, bound Maths inc/ntc_thermistor_math.hpp Ln16() , rounded and saturating integer helpers Types inc/ntc_thermistor_types.hpp Error , Result<T> , Curve , Config , Reading , Validate() Presets inc/ntc_thermistor_presets.hpp Two example curves, as data; included by nothing in the driver Port contract inc/ntc_thermistor_adc_interface.hpp The CRTP base and the AdcPort concept Platform port Your class ADC bring-up, one raw conversion, optional delay and bias The conversion is outside the class ¶ The conversion does not depend on the port, so it lives in free functions, not in the class template: it is compiled once per configuration, not once per port, can be used (and tested) with no port at all, and is evaluated at compile time when the inputs are constexpr . NtcThermistor<Port>::Read() is sampling around one call to it. From an ADC code to a temperature Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow hands one number to the next stage. Read() takes sample_count codes and their mean (the spread check can stop it as Unstable). The mean code is classified: at or above 2^bits is CodeOutOfScale, a code in the margin at the open rail is OpenCircuit, one in the margin at the short rail is ShortCircuit; which rail is which depends on the divider side. The node ratio gives the thermistor's resistance from the series resistor, in 1/256 ohm. The resistance goes through the curve: a table (a bounded binary search, then linear interpolation in ln R) or Steinhart-Hart (a cubic in ln R) or the beta equation (1/T in Q32), any of them with no floating point and no library. The temperature must lie inside the window; the offset is added last. The uncertainty bound is computed from the same code. The stages are the functions of inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp. Drawn from: inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp ConvertCode() ; inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp FineOfCode() ; inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp CurveTemperature() ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/conversion-pipeline.py . Rules the code keeps ¶ Integer only. Resistance in ohms (1/256 inside), temperature in milli-degrees, voltage in millivolts, tolerance in parts per million. No float , no double , no library math. A part is data. Nothing in inc/ or src/ names a part; the presets are Curve values. Bounded. Every loop has a constant bound: the table search is at most 8 steps, Ln16() a fixed number of steps. Port-independent code stays outside the class template. Next: Contract .

docs.text: Changelog ¶ What changed in each release of the driver. Entries under Breaking need source changes in code that used the affected API. [Unreleased] ¶ Added ¶ First version: a generic driver for NTC thermistors read through a resistor divider into an ADC port. NtcThermistor<Port> with EnsureInitialized() , Read() , ReadResistance() , ReadRawCode() , GetLastCode() , SetConfig() and GetConfig() ; the port needs EnsureInitialized() and ReadRaw() , and may add DelayUs() and SetBias() . Pure conversion functions with no port: Convert() , ConvertResistance() , ToMilliKelvin() , ToMilliFahrenheit() , SelfHeatingMicrowatts() and Validate() . All arithmetic is integer: no floating point, no libm. A part is data: a Curve that is a table of 2 to 256 rows (interpolated linearly in ln R), Steinhart-Hart coefficients ( sh_a_e15 , sh_b_e15 , sh_c_e15 , Q16 integer maths, with a mandatory valid window) or R25 and B (beta mode, likewise). tools/ntc_table.py makes and checks a table from coefficients, R25 and B, or a vendor list. Two presets: a generic 10 kOhm / B 3950 class and a TDK table (R25, B and tolerances checked against the vendor's Rev.3 datasheet; the rows are not, as the sheet prints no table). The bound uncertainty_mc is a bound on the declared tolerances: R, the series resistor, B (beta and table modes), curve_error_mc and one converter step. Both divider topologies, ratiometric or with separate supply and reference, open and short margins, averaging with a spread check, an optional bias switch (waits are capped at 1 s), and uncertainty_mc on every reading. With a reference above the supply the fault margins count from the highest code the supply can produce. Errors OpenCircuit , ShortCircuit , BelowRange , AboveRange , Unstable and CodeOutOfScale . Host tests against an independent seven-part model, a fuzz target, compile-fail tests, a host example and an ESP-IDF example.

docs.text: Contract ¶ What the NTC thermistor driver promises, what it needs, and the rules a caller follows. The driver inherits the Kokeb Labs driver contract ; this page states only what is specific to it. Promises ¶ The constructor is noexcept , stores the configuration, does no I/O and cannot fail. EnsureInitialized() checks the configuration (no I/O), brings the port's ADC up and, if the port has SetBias() , switches the divider off. A thermistor has no identity, so there is nothing to check on the part. Every read returns Error::NotInitialized before EnsureInitialized() succeeds and makes no port call. No call starts anything as a side effect. Convert() , ConvertResistance() and Validate() are pure: equal inputs, equal outputs, no state. All arithmetic is integer. No intermediate overflows or wraps: 64-bit intermediates are bounded by the limits Validate() enforces, and a result that does not fit saturates (the bound, the offset) or is an error (a resistance beyond 32 bits is BelowRange ). A read takes at most sample_count conversions. With SetBias() the order is on, settle, samples, off, convert, and the divider is off again on every path, including every error. A failed call returns an Error this driver returns and a zero value. Ok never comes from a failed sample, a sample at or above 2^ adc_bits , or samples whose spread is above max_spread_codes . An Ok temperature is inside the window (and, in table mode, inside the table's span) before the offset is added; uncertainty_mc is at least 1. A node at the open rail is never Ok and never reported as a short; the open and short margins follow the fault, not the rail, and swap with the topology. ReadRawCode() is a single-shot raw access: one conversion, no averaging, no retry, the same bias sequence; GetLastCode() returns the last code the port gave, with no I/O. Neither has a side effect on the part. Every port failure propagates as Error::Bus . There are no retries: a failed sample ends the read. A configuration the driver cannot honour (a wait the port cannot make, a beta or Steinhart-Hart curve without a window, an empty curve, a wait over one second) is InvalidArgument before any I/O. SetConfig() leaves the old configuration on failure. Depends on ¶ Dependency Version Why A C++20 compiler GCC 10, Clang 13 or later Concepts constrain the port CMake 3.16 or later Generates ntc_thermistor_version.h Your port The ADC, and optionally a delay and a GPIO that powers the divider There is no dependency on a math library, the C++ standard library's <cmath> or floating point. Threading ¶ Not thread-safe; takes no lock. One owner task, or one mutex around every call. Errors ¶ Error Value Returned when Ok 0 The call succeeded NotInitialized 1 Before EnsureInitialized() succeeded InvalidArgument 2 The configuration is not valid Bus 3 The port failed OpenCircuit 16 The node is at the open rail ShortCircuit 17 The node is at the short rail BelowRange 18 Colder than the curve or the window; or a resistance beyond 32 bits AboveRange 19 Hotter than the curve or the window; or a resistance of zero Unstable 20 The samples disagree by more than max_spread_codes CodeOutOfScale 21 A sample is at or above 2^ adc_bits Timeout , DeviceIdMismatch , Crc , Busy , DeviceFault and Unsupported are never returned; a test checks that every value above is returned by some call. Memory ¶ No heap, exceptions, RTTI or static mutable state. The object holds a port reference and a Config . A table is not copied: the span points at your array, which must outlive the driver. Platform ¶ Platform-free; the ESP-IDF port in examples/esp32 is an example. Deviations from the standard ¶ None.

docs.text: Conversion ¶ How a raw ADC code becomes a temperature, with integers only: the pipeline, the divider, the three ways to describe a part, how accurate each is, and how to make a table from any description or from a vendor list. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Public references n/a n/a: Beta equation and the B25/85 pair: Beta model, 1/T = 1/T0 + ln(R/R0) / B, p. 1 Steinhart-Hart and the table tool: Steinhart-Hart, 1/T = a + b ln R + c ln(R)^3, p. 1 Voltage divider and the series resistor: Divider, V = V_s R_n / (R_s + R_n), p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . From an ADC code to a temperature Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow hands one number to the next stage. Read() takes sample_count codes and their mean (the spread check can stop it as Unstable). The mean code is classified: at or above 2^bits is CodeOutOfScale, a code in the margin at the open rail is OpenCircuit, one in the margin at the short rail is ShortCircuit; which rail is which depends on the divider side. The node ratio gives the thermistor's resistance from the series resistor, in 1/256 ohm. The resistance goes through the curve: a table (a bounded binary search, then linear interpolation in ln R) or Steinhart-Hart (a cubic in ln R) or the beta equation (1/T in Q32), any of them with no floating point and no library. The temperature must lie inside the window; the offset is added last. The uncertainty bound is computed from the same code. The stages are the functions of inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp. Drawn from: inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp ConvertCode() ; inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp FineOfCode() ; inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp CurveTemperature() ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/conversion-pipeline.py . All quantities are integers: resistance in ohms, temperature in milli-degrees Celsius, voltage in millivolts, tolerance in parts per million. There is no floating point and no library call ( libm is not linked); the logarithm is an integer function, Ln16() , accurate to within one unit of 2^-16 neper over 1 to 2^64 - 1 (measured 0.77 unit), with its own test. 1. The code ¶ Read() takes sample_count conversions, each checked: a code at or above 2^ adc_bits is CodeOutOfScale . The mean is (sum + count / 2) / count . If max_spread_codes is set and the largest sample minus the smallest is more, the reading is Unstable . The code is a number of ADC steps; the driver treats a node ratio as code / 2^bits (one step different from code / (2^bits - 1) , which is inside the quantisation; pinned by a test, not verified on hardware ). 2. Classifying the code ¶ Before any arithmetic the driver rules out the codes that cannot be a thermistor: Code Low-side divider High-side divider Within open_margin_codes of full scale OpenCircuit ShortCircuit Within short_margin_codes of zero ShortCircuit OpenCircuit The margins belong to the fault, not to the rail: they swap with the topology. When the reference is above the divider supply the node cannot read above 2^bits * supply / reference : the margin at the open (or short) rail is counted from that code, not from the converter's top code. With 12 bits, a 3300 mV reference and a 3000 mV supply the node tops out at code 3723, so with the default margin of 2 the codes from 3720 up are the fault. The margins are in codes, so on a 20-bit or wider converter two codes are noise: choose them from the noise of the node (see Reference and supplies ). 3. From the node to a resistance ¶ With r = code / 2^bits (or code / 2^bits * vref / supply when the reference and the supply differ): low side: Rn = Rs * r / (1 - r) high side: Rn = Rs * (1 - r) / r The driver carries the resistance in 1/256 ohm ("fine ohms") rounded to nearest. Whole ohms would cost as much as an ADC step at the hot end of a low-resistance part. A resistance that does not fit 32 bits is BelowRange ; zero is AboveRange . 4. From a resistance to a temperature ¶ A curve is exactly one of a table, Steinhart-Hart coefficients, or R25 and B. All are data: a non-empty table selects table mode, otherwise a non-zero sh_b_e15 selects Steinhart-Hart mode, otherwise it is beta mode. Table mode ¶ 2 to 256 rows, any spacing, resistance strictly falling as temperature strictly rises. The driver finds the segment by a binary search of at most 8 steps, then interpolates linearly in ln R , which follows the real curve far better than linear in R: T = Ta + (Tb - Ta) * (ln Ra - ln R) / (ln Ra - ln Rb) Above the first row's resistance is BelowRange (colder than the table), below the last row's is AboveRange . There is no extrapolation. A row is exact: a resistance equal to a row's returns that row's temperature. An end of the table is a hard edge: a node a fraction of an ADC step beyond the first or last row is a range error, not the end temperature. Extend the table (the generator takes --from and --to ) so that the part's rated range lies inside it. The step rule. The interpolation error grows with the square of the row spacing. For tables built from a beta curve the worst error over a segment was measured at 0.105 K for 10 degree rows, 0.027 K for 5 degree rows and 0.007 K for 2.5 degree rows, so it is bounded by 0.0013 * step^2 + 0.003 kelvin, step in degrees (the model pins this in tests/test_model.cpp ). A table with rows every 5 degrees or less is within about one ADC step of the curve on a 12-bit ADC; rows every 10 degrees or more make the table the dominant error. Steinhart-Hart mode ¶ 1/T = A + B ln R + C (ln R)^3 (T in kelvin, R in ohms) The coefficients are Curve::sh_a_e15 , sh_b_e15 and sh_c_e15 , integers in units of 1e-15 per kelvin: a vendor's A = 0.8767633e-3 is 876'763'300'000 , B = 2.527899e-4 is 252'789'900'000 , C = 1.906681e-7 is 190'668'100 . A non-zero sh_b_e15 selects the mode; r0_ohm , b_kelvin and b_tol_ppm must then be 0 (one description only). Validate() requires bounded coefficients, 1/T rising with ln R over the whole resistance range (B > 0, and B + 3 C ln(R)^2 > 0 at the largest ln R), and a window, as for beta mode: the polynomial extrapolates. The maths is Q16 arithmetic on Ln16() : the cube is formed in two Q16 products and the temperature is 10^18 / (1/T in 1e-15) in milli-kelvin, so it is measured within 5 mK of the equation over -40 to 150 degrees Celsius (10 mK in a randomised check of other coefficient sets up to 300 degrees Celsius, against an independent Python evaluation). An inverse that is not positive is AboveRange . The coefficients carry no tolerance: put the fit's error into curve_error_mc . This is the three-coefficient form with R in ohms. A vendor that publishes a four-term polynomial, ln R of R in kilo-ohms or another R0 normalisation needs its coefficients converted, or a table: tools/ntc_table.py list makes one from the vendor's own resistance and temperature list, with no model at all. Beta mode ¶ 1/T = 1/T0 + ln(R / R0) / B (T in kelvin) R0 is r0_ohm at ref_temperature_mc (25 degrees Celsius for nearly every part) and B is b_kelvin ; the sum is computed in Q32 fixed point. Beta mode requires a window , min_temperature_mc and max_temperature_mc : the equation is a two-point fit and extrapolates without complaint, so the driver will not guess the range for you. A temperature outside the window is BelowRange or AboveRange . b_t2_mc records the second temperature of the B pair you took B from (85 degrees Celsius for B25/85); it is validated but does not enter the arithmetic. Beta fits a real part exactly at the two temperatures of its pair and drifts away from them. Use it when the part's datasheet gives only R25 and B, over a range near the pair; use a table when it gives a table. 5. Window, offset, bound ¶ The temperature must lie in [min_temperature_mc, max_temperature_mc] ; then offset_mc is added (saturating). Reading::uncertainty_mc is a worst-case linear sum, at least 1 and saturating, of: the tolerance of R ( r_tol_ppm ): the temperature at R * (1 + tol) and R * (1 - tol) , rounded outward; the same for the series resistor ( series_tol_ppm ); the tolerance of B ( b_tol_ppm ), in beta mode and in table mode: T^2 * |1/T - 1/T0| * tol , which is T^2 * |ln(R / R0)| / B * tol for a beta curve and uses the table's own implied B at this point for a table ( T0 is ref_temperature_mc ); it is zero at the reference temperature and about 1.3 K at 125 degrees Celsius for 1 %; the error of the curve itself ( curve_error_mc ): the fit error of Steinhart-Hart coefficients, or the interpolation error of a table (the generator prints it); one ADC step, from the neighbouring codes. A tolerance of 0 means "not declared" and adds nothing; with nothing declared the bound is one converter code. It is a bound on the declared tolerances, not a guarantee about the part: the tolerance of R is applied as the same ratio at every temperature, whereas a vendor's tolerance grows away from 25 degrees Celsius (declare the largest). It does not include self-heating, the ADC's own gain and offset errors, or a filter that has not settled. Beta against a table, the same part ¶ The case for tables, on the worked example (the rows of the example preset, unverified, against a beta curve with B25/85 = 3435 K, R25 = 10 kOhm; error = beta minus table): Temperature (degC) Table (degC) Beta (degC) Beta error (K) -35 -35.03 -31.12 +3.88 -20 -20.02 -17.50 +2.50 0 0.01 1.12 +1.12 25 25.00 25.00 0.00 50 50.00 49.58 -0.42 85 85.00 85.01 +0.01 100 99.99 100.48 +0.48 125 124.92 126.60 +1.60 145 144.99 147.95 +2.95 Beta is right where its pair is and wrong by a few kelvin at the ends. The table follows the part. The same conclusion holds for any part whose real curve is not a single beta: see Worked example . Making a table ¶ A table is the form every part can take. tools/ntc_table.py makes one, checks it the way Validate() does, and prints the interpolation error against the source curve: # Steinhart-Hart coefficients (a datasheet's or a calibration's) python3 tools/ntc_table.py sh 0 .8767633e-3 2 .527899e-4 1 .906681e-7 --from -40 --to 150 --step 5 --name kMyPart # R25 and B python3 tools/ntc_table.py beta 10000 3950 --from -40 --to 125 --step 5 # A vendor's list: lines of "temperature_degC resistance_ohm" python3 tools/ntc_table.py list vendor_table.txt --name kMyPart It prints a constexpr array of TablePoint , then a comment with the row count, the range, and the measured error at the middle of every segment. It exits non-zero when the table would be refused: fewer than 2 or more than 256 rows, a resistance that does not fall strictly after rounding to whole ohms, two rows whose logarithms agree to 2^-16, a resistance that does not fit 1 to 2^32 - 1. --max-error K fails a table whose error is above K . docs.text: How a raw ADC code becomes a temperature, with integers only: the pipeline, the divider, the three ways to describe a part, how accurate each is, and how to make a table from any description or from a vendor list. Datasheet sections this page relies on From Public references n/a n/a: Beta equation and the B25/85 pair: Beta model, 1/T = 1/T0 + ln(R/R0) / B, p. 1 Steinhart-Hart and the table tool: Steinhart-Hart, 1/T = a + b ln R + c ln(R)^3, p. 1 Voltage divider and the series resistor: Divider, V = V_s R_n / (R_s + R_n), p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . From an ADC code to a temperature Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow hands one number to the next stage. Read() takes sample_count codes and their mean (the spread check can stop it as Unstable). The mean code is classified: at or above 2^bits is CodeOutOfScale, a code in the margin at the open rail is OpenCircuit, one in the margin at the short rail is ShortCircuit; which rail is which depends on the divider side. The node ratio gives the thermistor's resistance from the series resistor, in 1/256 ohm. The resistance goes through the curve: a table (a bounded binary search, then linear interpolation in ln R) or Steinhart-Hart (a cubic in ln R) or the beta equation (1/T in Q32), any of them with no floating point and no library. The temperature must lie inside the window; the offset is added last. The uncertainty bound is computed from the same code. The stages are the functions of inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp. Drawn from: inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp ConvertCode() ; inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp FineOfCode() ; inc/ntc_thermistor_conversion.hpp CurveTemperature() ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/conversion-pipeline.py . All quantities are integers: resistance in ohms, temperature in milli-degrees Celsius, voltage in millivolts, tolerance in parts per million. There is no floating point and no library call ( libm is not linked); the logarithm is an integer function, Ln16() , accurate to within one unit of 2^-16 neper over 1 to 2^64 - 1 (measured 0.77 unit), with its own test.
docs.title: Conversion

docs.text: Read() takes sample_count conversions, each checked: a code at or above 2^ adc_bits is CodeOutOfScale . The mean is (sum + count / 2) / count . If max_spread_codes is set and the largest sample minus the smallest is more, the reading is Unstable . The code is a number of ADC steps; the driver treats a node ratio as code / 2^bits (one step different from code / (2^bits - 1) , which is inside the quantisation; pinned by a test, not verified on hardware ).
docs.title: 1. The code

docs.text: Before any arithmetic the driver rules out the codes that cannot be a thermistor: Code Low-side divider High-side divider Within open_margin_codes of full scale OpenCircuit ShortCircuit Within short_margin_codes of zero ShortCircuit OpenCircuit The margins belong to the fault, not to the rail: they swap with the topology. When the reference is above the divider supply the node cannot read above 2^bits * supply / reference : the margin at the open (or short) rail is counted from that code, not from the converter's top code. With 12 bits, a 3300 mV reference and a 3000 mV supply the node tops out at code 3723, so with the default margin of 2 the codes from 3720 up are the fault. The margins are in codes, so on a 20-bit or wider converter two codes are noise: choose them from the noise of the node (see Reference and supplies ).
docs.title: 2. Classifying the code

docs.text: With r = code / 2^bits (or code / 2^bits * vref / supply when the reference and the supply differ): low side: Rn = Rs * r / (1 - r) high side: Rn = Rs * (1 - r) / r The driver carries the resistance in 1/256 ohm ("fine ohms") rounded to nearest. Whole ohms would cost as much as an ADC step at the hot end of a low-resistance part. A resistance that does not fit 32 bits is BelowRange ; zero is AboveRange .
docs.title: 3. From the node to a resistance

docs.text: A curve is exactly one of a table, Steinhart-Hart coefficients, or R25 and B. All are data: a non-empty table selects table mode, otherwise a non-zero sh_b_e15 selects Steinhart-Hart mode, otherwise it is beta mode.
docs.title: 4. From a resistance to a temperature

docs.text: 2 to 256 rows, any spacing, resistance strictly falling as temperature strictly rises. The driver finds the segment by a binary search of at most 8 steps, then interpolates linearly in ln R , which follows the real curve far better than linear in R: T = Ta + (Tb - Ta) * (ln Ra - ln R) / (ln Ra - ln Rb) Above the first row's resistance is BelowRange (colder than the table), below the last row's is AboveRange . There is no extrapolation. A row is exact: a resistance equal to a row's returns that row's temperature. An end of the table is a hard edge: a node a fraction of an ADC step beyond the first or last row is a range error, not the end temperature. Extend the table (the generator takes --from and --to ) so that the part's rated range lies inside it. The step rule. The interpolation error grows with the square of the row spacing. For tables built from a beta curve the worst error over a segment was measured at 0.105 K for 10 degree rows, 0.027 K for 5 degree rows and 0.007 K for 2.5 degree rows, so it is bounded by 0.0013 * step^2 + 0.003 kelvin, step in degrees (the model pins this in tests/test_model.cpp ). A table with rows every 5 degrees or less is within about one ADC step of the curve on a 12-bit ADC; rows every 10 degrees or more make the table the dominant error.
docs.title: Table mode

docs.text: 1/T = A + B ln R + C (ln R)^3 (T in kelvin, R in ohms) The coefficients are Curve::sh_a_e15 , sh_b_e15 and sh_c_e15 , integers in units of 1e-15 per kelvin: a vendor's A = 0.8767633e-3 is 876'763'300'000 , B = 2.527899e-4 is 252'789'900'000 , C = 1.906681e-7 is 190'668'100 . A non-zero sh_b_e15 selects the mode; r0_ohm , b_kelvin and b_tol_ppm must then be 0 (one description only). Validate() requires bounded coefficients, 1/T rising with ln R over the whole resistance range (B > 0, and B + 3 C ln(R)^2 > 0 at the largest ln R), and a window, as for beta mode: the polynomial extrapolates. The maths is Q16 arithmetic on Ln16() : the cube is formed in two Q16 products and the temperature is 10^18 / (1/T in 1e-15) in milli-kelvin, so it is measured within 5 mK of the equation over -40 to 150 degrees Celsius (10 mK in a randomised check of other coefficient sets up to 300 degrees Celsius, against an independent Python evaluation). An inverse that is not positive is AboveRange . The coefficients carry no tolerance: put the fit's error into curve_error_mc . This is the three-coefficient form with R in ohms. A vendor that publishes a four-term polynomial, ln R of R in kilo-ohms or another R0 normalisation needs its coefficients converted, or a table: tools/ntc_table.py list makes one from the vendor's own resistance and temperature list, with no model at all.
docs.title: Steinhart-Hart mode

docs.text: 1/T = 1/T0 + ln(R / R0) / B (T in kelvin) R0 is r0_ohm at ref_temperature_mc (25 degrees Celsius for nearly every part) and B is b_kelvin ; the sum is computed in Q32 fixed point. Beta mode requires a window , min_temperature_mc and max_temperature_mc : the equation is a two-point fit and extrapolates without complaint, so the driver will not guess the range for you. A temperature outside the window is BelowRange or AboveRange . b_t2_mc records the second temperature of the B pair you took B from (85 degrees Celsius for B25/85); it is validated but does not enter the arithmetic. Beta fits a real part exactly at the two temperatures of its pair and drifts away from them. Use it when the part's datasheet gives only R25 and B, over a range near the pair; use a table when it gives a table.
docs.title: Beta mode

docs.text: The temperature must lie in [min_temperature_mc, max_temperature_mc] ; then offset_mc is added (saturating). Reading::uncertainty_mc is a worst-case linear sum, at least 1 and saturating, of: the tolerance of R ( r_tol_ppm ): the temperature at R * (1 + tol) and R * (1 - tol) , rounded outward; the same for the series resistor ( series_tol_ppm ); the tolerance of B ( b_tol_ppm ), in beta mode and in table mode: T^2 * |1/T - 1/T0| * tol , which is T^2 * |ln(R / R0)| / B * tol for a beta curve and uses the table's own implied B at this point for a table ( T0 is ref_temperature_mc ); it is zero at the reference temperature and about 1.3 K at 125 degrees Celsius for 1 %; the error of the curve itself ( curve_error_mc ): the fit error of Steinhart-Hart coefficients, or the interpolation error of a table (the generator prints it); one ADC step, from the neighbouring codes. A tolerance of 0 means "not declared" and adds nothing; with nothing declared the bound is one converter code. It is a bound on the declared tolerances, not a guarantee about the part: the tolerance of R is applied as the same ratio at every temperature, whereas a vendor's tolerance grows away from 25 degrees Celsius (declare the largest). It does not include self-heating, the ADC's own gain and offset errors, or a filter that has not settled.

docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake project on any MCU or on your PC, or to an ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++20 library with no dependencies, and one root CMakeLists.txt serves every build. Requirements ¶ A C++20 compiler: GCC 10+, Clang 13+ or a current MSVC. The driver uses concepts and requires . CMake 3.16 or later: it generates the version header the driver includes ( ntc_thermistor_version.h ). No RTOS, heap, exceptions or RTTI: every call is noexcept and returns a Result . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to the version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-ntc-thermistor.git external/driver-ntc-thermistor git submodule update --init external/driver-ntc-thermistor Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ , _config/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples are not; the ESP32 example even has its own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ). CMake (any MCU, any host) ¶ This is the MCU-neutral path: the same two lines work for a host build, STM32 (CubeMX CMake projects), RP2040 (Pico SDK), nRF (nRF Connect SDK) or any other CMake toolchain. Platforms lists what has a port today. add_subdirectory ( external/driver-ntc-thermistor ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE ntc_thermistor::ntc_thermistor ) ntc_thermistor::ntc_thermistor is an alias of the ntc_thermistor INTERFACE target. It carries the include directories (the headers and the generated version header) and requires C++20, so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect NTC_THERMISTOR_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on every target that links the driver NTC_THERMISTOR_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host tests in tests/ and the host example ( Testing and CI ) Installed package ¶ To use the driver without adding its source tree to your build, install it and find the package: cmake -S external/driver-ntc-thermistor -B build-ntc_thermistor cmake --install build-ntc_thermistor --prefix /opt/sdk find_package ( ntc_thermistor 0.1 REQUIRED ) # with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/sdk target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE ntc_thermistor::ntc_thermistor ) The target is ntc_thermistor::ntc_thermistor in both cases ( EXPORT_NAME ), so a project can switch between add_subdirectory() and find_package() without changing its target_link_libraries() . The headers and the generated ntc_thermistor_version.h go to include/ntc_thermistor/inc/ , the template implementation to include/ntc_thermistor/src/ntc_thermistor.ipp . The host CI installs the package and builds a consumer against it on every pull request ( Testing and CI ). ESP-IDF ¶ Under ESP-IDF the root CMakeLists.txt registers the repository itself as a component: with ESP_PLATFORM set it calls idf_component_register() from the same build settings, with the menu in _config/Kconfig . There is no wrapper to copy. ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so the name in your REQUIRES is the name of the folder the repository is in. Pick one of these: How What to write Component name Folder of extra components list(APPEND EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS external/driver-ntc-thermistor) in the project CMakeLists.txt , before project.cmake driver-ntc-thermistor (the folder) Submodule under components/ git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-ntc-thermistor.git components/ntc_thermistor ntc_thermistor (the folder) Component manager, from git The dependency below in main/idf_component.yml ntc_thermistor (the key) # main/idf_component.yml of your project dependencies : ntc_thermistor : git : https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-ntc-thermistor.git version : v0.1.0 # a release tag Your component then declares REQUIRES ntc_thermistor (or the folder name), and idf.py menuconfig shows the driver's menu ( Configuration ). The ESP32 example uses the first way, with EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS pointing at the repository root, and works out the folder name in main/CMakeLists.txt ; CI builds it on every pull request. The repository has no idf_component.yml . The component manager does not need one for a git dependency; the manifest is only required to publish to the ESP Component Registry, which these releases do not use. If registry publishing is chosen, the manifest is added at the root then. How the build is organised ¶ Layer File Role Settings cmake/ntc_thermistor_build_settings.cmake Target name, include directories, sources, version: the single source of truth Library CMakeLists.txt INTERFACE target, alias, install rules and the package export, or the ESP-IDF component Tool configuration _config/ Doxyfile, the docs site, Kconfig, clang-format, clang-tidy and the linters Version ¶ The version is set once in the settings file and written into ntc_thermistor_version.h in the build tree at configure time. The Doxyfile ( _config/Doxyfile ) carries a copy; a host test fails when it differs. Read it at run time: const char * v = ntc_thermistor :: GetDriverVersion (); // "0.1.0" Next ¶ Quickstart runs the driver on your PC, then on your MCU; Porting writes the port for your MCU.

docs.text: To use the driver without adding its source tree to your build, install it and find the package: cmake -S external/driver-ntc-thermistor -B build-ntc_thermistor cmake --install build-ntc_thermistor --prefix /opt/sdk find_package ( ntc_thermistor 0.1 REQUIRED ) # with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/sdk target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE ntc_thermistor::ntc_thermistor ) The target is ntc_thermistor::ntc_thermistor in both cases ( EXPORT_NAME ), so a project can switch between add_subdirectory() and find_package() without changing its target_link_libraries() . docs.text: Under ESP-IDF the root CMakeLists.txt registers the repository itself as a component: with ESP_PLATFORM set it calls idf_component_register() from the same build settings, with the menu in _config/Kconfig . There is no wrapper to copy. ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so the name in your REQUIRES is the name of the folder the repository is in. Pick one of these: How What to write Component name Folder of extra components list(APPEND EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS external/driver-ntc-thermistor) in the project CMakeLists.txt , before project.cmake driver-ntc-thermistor (the folder) Submodule under components/ git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-ntc-thermistor.git components/ntc_thermistor ntc_thermistor (the folder) Component manager, from git The dependency below in main/idf_component.yml ntc_thermistor (the key) # main/idf_component.yml of your project dependencies : ntc_thermistor : git : https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-ntc-thermistor.git version : v0.1.0 # a release tag Your component then declares REQUIRES ntc_thermistor (or the folder name), and idf.py menuconfig shows the driver's menu ( Configuration ). docs.text: Status and limitations ¶ What the driver does not do, what is unverified, and what would settle each. Not verified on hardware ¶ The driver is host-tested against a model of the divider and fuzzed. It has not been run on a thermistor. The bench steps that would settle it: read a known part at an ice bath, room temperature and a warm bath with a reference thermometer and compare with the bound; cut the thermistor and short it and see OpenCircuit and ShortCircuit ; power the divider from a GPIO and check the settle time against the filter. The ratio convention ( code / 2^bits against code / (2^bits - 1) ) is inside the quantisation and pinned by a test; it is not verified on hardware. The example preset's rows are unverified ¶ The TDK NTCG163JF103FT1S datasheet (Rev.3, 2023-05-08) confirms R25, B and the tolerances, but it prints no resistance table: the table is a separate step file that answers 403 to an automated fetch. The 39 rows are a secondary listing, consistent with the sheet's B values, and are not checked row by row. See Presets and Worked example . Nothing generic depends on it. What the driver does not do ¶ Floating point and libm. Everything is integer. Steinhart-Hart is a run-time mode (Q16 arithmetic, a cubic and an inverse) in its three-coefficient form with R in ohms; for a four-term polynomial, another unit or another normalisation, tools/ntc_table.py list makes a table from the vendor's own list. Filtering. Averaging is the driver's; an exponential or other filter across readings is application policy. Self-heating correction. The power is computed ( Hardware ); the dissipation constant is yours and is not applied. SelfHeatingMicrowatts() returns 0 for a ratiometric configuration (the supply is unknown), which is the same number as "no heating", and rounds twice, so it can be 1 microwatt off at small power. Telling a collapsed supply from a short on a low-side divider. Extrapolation. Outside a table or a window is an error, not a guess. A table end is a hard edge: a node a fraction of an ADC step beyond the first or last row is a range error. Extend the table. A parallel (linearisation) resistor across the thermistor. Tabulate the network: give tools/ntc_table.py a list of the parallel resistance at each temperature. Fractional ohms in a table. TablePoint::resistance_ohm is whole ohms, so a part below about 10 ohm (inrush limiters, a hot end below 1 ohm) is outside the useful range. The bounds are r0_ohm 1 to 10 MOhm, b_kelvin 1000 to 8000, a series resistor to 16 MOhm, a resistance below 2^32 ohm. A cut wire between the node and the ADC pin. A floating input reads whatever it last held; the driver cannot tell it from a temperature. A pull resistor at the pin (or a second reading with the divider off) is yours. Calibrating the ADC. The driver takes a raw count and a full scale. Thread safety. One owner task per object. Beta B in finer units. b_kelvin is an integer; a part that quotes a decimal B rounds, under 0.01 K at the ends. What the bound is ¶ Reading::uncertainty_mc is a bound on the tolerances you declare, as a linear sum: R, the series resistor, B (beta and table modes), curve_error_mc and one converter step. It applies the tolerance of R as one ratio at every temperature, where a vendor's tolerance grows away from 25 degrees Celsius: declare the largest. A part whose B tolerance is not declared adds nothing for it. Waits are bounded ¶ sample_delay_us and settle_us are at most 1 000 000 microseconds each ( Validate() refuses more), so one Read() takes at most settle_us + (sample_count - 1) * sample_delay_us of waiting, 16 seconds in the worst case. Choices the owner can change ¶ Each is a small change if the default is not wanted: a fixed-point filter helper outside the class; the divider's code convention; a series-resistor helper in code (the rule is in Hardware ); a dissipation_uw_per_k field with a correction flag; a tolerance in codes or ohms before a table end becomes a range error; the removal of uncertainty_mc from Reading .

docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: the port. The driver calls hooks on a class you derive from ntc_thermistor::AdcInterface<Self> (in inc/ntc_thermistor_adc_interface.hpp ). The base declares no hook; the driver template is constrained by the ntc_thermistor::AdcPort concept, so a missing or misdeclared hook is a compile error with a message that names it. What you implement ¶ Method Required Contract bool EnsureInitialized() noexcept yes Bring the ADC up on the first call; true at once afterwards bool ReadRaw(uint8_t channel, uint32_t& code) noexcept yes One conversion of channel : the raw count, 0 to 2^ adc_bits - 1; no averaging, no volts; false on any failure void DelayUs(uint32_t us) noexcept only if the configuration waits Wait at least us microseconds ( sample_delay_us , settle_us ) bool SetBias(bool on) noexcept no Power the divider only while sampling; false when the pin could not be driven Optional hooks are found by name at compile time and must have exactly these signatures; a hook with the right name and a wrong signature (a narrowed parameter, a missing noexcept , a void return) does not compile. The driver refuses at EnsureInitialized() a configuration that waits for something the port cannot do: a sample_delay_us or settle_us without DelayUs() , or a settle_us without SetBias() . The port ¶ my_port.hpp class MyPort : public ntc_thermistor :: AdcInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the ADC up once; later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_adc_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One conversion of `channel`: the raw count, as many bits as // Config::adc_bits says. No averaging. bool ReadRaw ( uint8_t channel , uint32_t & code ) noexcept { return platform_adc_read_raw ( channel , code ); } // Optional: wait at least `us` microseconds (sample_delay_us, settle_us). void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; A port with every hook, powering the divider from a GPIO only while it is read (which also removes the self-heating between readings): // A port with both optional hooks: the divider is powered from a GPIO only // while sampling. class FullPort : public ntc_thermistor :: AdcInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_adc_init (); } bool ReadRaw ( uint8_t channel , uint32_t & code ) noexcept { return platform_adc_read_raw ( channel , code ); } void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } // true when the pin was driven; the driver treats false as Bus and still // switches the divider off. bool SetBias ( bool on ) noexcept { platform_gpio_write ( kBiasPin , on ); return true ; } private : static constexpr int kBiasPin = 4 ; }; Bias ¶ When the port has SetBias() , every Read() runs this order: on, settle, samples, off, convert . The divider is switched off on every path, including a failed switch-on, a failed sample, an out-of-scale code and Unstable . EnsureInitialized() also switches it off once, so the first reading starts from a known state. A failed switch-off after a good read is Bus : a divider left on is a fault. There are no retries. The pin's idle level is "off": set it before the output is enabled (handbook KB-HW-018), or the divider glitches on at start-up. A port for a board where the divider is always powered either leaves SetBias() out (then settle_us must be 0) or provides it as a successful no-op, as the ESP32 example does when no GPIO is set: a SetBias() that returns false is a Bus error at EnsureInitialized() . Codes and millivolts ¶ Return the raw count. If your SDK gives only calibrated millivolts, map them back to a code of adc_bits bits over the full scale and declare that full scale (see Reference, range and supplies ): // A port that only has calibrated millivolts: map them back to a code of // `adc_bits` bits. bool platform_adc_read_mv ( uint8_t channel , uint32_t & millivolts ) noexcept ; class MillivoltPort : public ntc_thermistor :: AdcInterface < MillivoltPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return true ; } bool ReadRaw ( uint8_t channel , uint32_t & code ) noexcept { uint32_t mv = 0 ; if ( ! platform_adc_read_mv ( channel , mv )) { return false ; } code = ( mv * 4096U ) / 3300U ; // 12 bits over the 3.3 V full scale: loses under one code code = ( code > 4095U ) ? 4095U : code ; return true ; } }; The ESP32 example, esp32_ntc_thermistor_port.hpp , uses the one-shot ADC and an optional GPIO. Describing your part and your hardware ¶ Porting also covers the documentation of a board: Hardware has the recipe for adapting hardware.yml and the chip card to your thermistor, and Presets how to declare the part as data. Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each driver object one owner task, or guard every call with one mutex.

docs.text: Presets ¶ A preset is a Curve the driver ships as an example. The driver includes the presets header nowhere; a part is added by writing a Curve , never by changing the driver. Datasheet sections this page relies on Beta equation and the B25/85 pair: Public references n/a n/a, Beta model, 1/T = 1/T0 + ln(R/R0) / B, p. 1 Steinhart-Hart and the table tool: Public references n/a n/a, Steinhart-Hart, 1/T = a + b ln R + c ln(R)^3, p. 1 Example part: R-T table (rows unverified): TDK none printed Rev.3, Electrical Characteristics, 1degC Step Data link (the table itself is not in the PDF), p. 1 Example part: R25, B and tolerances: TDK none printed Rev.3, Electrical Characteristics: Resistance, B value, p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . #include "ntc_thermistor_presets.hpp" Preset Mode R25 B Source Status presets::kGeneric10kB3950 Beta 10 kOhm 3950 K (B25/50) Typical values of the common 10 kOhm / 3950 K class Typical, not a datasheet claim presets::kTdkNtcg163jf103ft1s Table, 39 rows, -40 to +150 degC every 5 10 kOhm 3435 K (B25/85) The worked example's TDK NTCG163JF103FT1S R25, B, tolerances: TDK Rev.3, p. 1. Rows: unverified Neither carries a window. A beta curve needs min_temperature_mc and max_temperature_mc in the Config ; a table carries its own range. The rows are unverified The datasheet of kTdkNtcg163jf103ft1s (TDK, Rev.3, 8 May 2023, one page) confirms R25 10 kOhm +-1 %, B25/85 3435 K +-1 %, B25/50 3380 K typ. and the range -40 to +150 degrees Celsius. It prints no resistance table : the step data is a separate file (403 to an automated fetch). The 39 rows are a secondary listing, consistent with those B values (a test checks it) but not compared row by row. A TDK NTCG163JF103FT1 (the 125 degree grade) is another part: verify against its own sheet. Do not rely on the rows for a product until you have compared them with the vendor's step file; the driver and its tests do not depend on them, and the rest of these pages hold for any part. The generic preset is a convenience There is no single datasheet behind "10 kOhm, B 3950": it is the typical value of a class sold as probes and beads. Wire it ¶ MCU Divider Notes ADC input Node between the series resistor and the thermistor The thermistor goes to ground (low side) 3.3 V Series resistor, 10 k as a start The same rail as the ADC reference, so the reading is ratiometric GND Thermistor Same ground as the ADC The Hardware page says how to choose the series resistor and what to do about the ADC input. 2. Add the driver ¶ git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-ntc-thermistor.git external/driver-ntc-thermistor 3. Write the port ¶ Two functions, one optional: bring the ADC up, and read one raw count of one channel. my_port.hpp class MyPort : public ntc_thermistor :: AdcInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the ADC up once; later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_adc_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One conversion of `channel`: the raw count, as many bits as // Config::adc_bits says. No averaging. bool ReadRaw ( uint8_t channel , uint32_t & code ) noexcept { return platform_adc_read_raw ( channel , code ); } // Optional: wait at least `us` microseconds (sample_delay_us, settle_us). void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; 4. Read the temperature ¶ main.cpp #include "ntc_thermistor.hpp" #include "ntc_thermistor_presets.hpp" // A 10 kOhm / B 3950 thermistor low-side in a 10 kOhm divider on a 12-bit ADC, // valid from -40 to +125 degC. constexpr ntc_thermistor :: Config kConfig {. curve = ntc_thermistor :: presets :: kGeneric10kB3950 , . min_temperature_mc = -40'000 , . max_temperature_mc = 125'000 }; int read_temperature_mc ( MyPort & port , int32_t & milli_celsius ) { ntc_thermistor :: NtcThermistor < MyPort > sensor ( port , kConfig ); // no I/O yet if ( auto r = sensor . EnsureInitialized (); ! r ) { // 1. check the config, bring the ADC up return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); // InvalidArgument or Bus } const auto t = sensor . Read (); // 2. sample, divider to ohms, curve to temperature if ( ! t ) { return static_cast < int > ( t . error ); // OpenCircuit, ShortCircuit, BelowRange, ... } milli_celsius = t . value . temperature_mc ; // 3. milli-degrees Celsius; // t.value.uncertainty_mc bounds it return 0 ; } Config has no default part : you name one. EnsureInitialized() checks the configuration (no I/O), brings the ADC up and switches the divider off. It is the only call that starts anything. Read() takes sample_count conversions, averages them, finds the resistance and the temperature, and returns a Reading : temperature_mc , resistance_ohm , code and uncertainty_mc . docs.text: Reference, range and supplies ¶ The divider and the ADC share a voltage, or they do not. This page says which case you have, what to declare, and how to keep the node inside the ADC's range. Ratiometric: the common case ¶ If the divider's supply is the ADC's reference (a MCU whose ADC measures against its own 3.3 V, with the divider on the same rail), the code is a pure ratio and the voltage drops out. Leave adc_vref_mv and divider_supply_mv at 0. Noise on the supply moves both together. Not ratiometric ¶ If the reference is another voltage (an ADC with an internal 1.1 V, 2.5 V or 3.3 V reference; a divider on 5 V read by a 3.3 V ADC), set both : divider_supply_mv : the voltage the divider is powered from; adc_vref_mv : the ADC's full scale. The node share is then code / 2^bits * vref / supply . If the supply is larger than the reference, choose the series resistor so that the node stays below the reference over the whole temperature range. When the reference is above the supply, the node cannot read above the code 2^bits * supply / reference , and the margin of the open rail (or the short rail of a high-side divider) is counted down from there: a 12-bit converter with a 3300 mV reference on a 3000 mV supply tops out at code 3723, and with the default margin of 2 the codes from 3720 up are the fault. configuration.cpp // A 5 V divider read by an ADC with a 3.3 V reference: the driver needs both // voltages. The node must stay inside the ADC's range: choose the series // resistor so that 5 V * node share stays below 3.3 V. inline constexpr ntc_thermistor :: Config kFiveVolts { . curve = ntc_thermistor :: presets :: kTdkNtcg163jf103ft1s , . series_ohm = 20'000 , . adc_vref_mv = 3300 , . divider_supply_mv = 5000 , . open_margin_codes = 4 , . short_margin_codes = 4 }; With a separate reference the open and short margins must be at least 1 code: a code at the very rail cannot be told from a wrong supply value. The conversion depends on the two voltages directly: a 1 % error in divider_supply_mv is a 1 % error in the node share, which is more than a degree at the ends of a part. Measure the supply or use a ratiometric divider. An ADC that is not linear to its reference ¶ Some ADCs (for example a microcontroller ADC with attenuation) have a full scale that depends on a setting and a transfer curve that is not exactly straight. The driver takes a raw count and a full scale in millivolts: it does not calibrate. Either calibrate in the port (return a code scaled to the full scale), or declare the effective full scale from a measurement of your board. The ESP32 example does the second and says so in its README. Range ¶ The node is at its middle where the thermistor equals the series resistor. The usable range of the part is where the node is not within the margins of a rail and where one ADC step is worth less than the accuracy you need: Hardware . A supply that collapses ¶ A low-side divider whose supply has collapsed reads as a short (the node is at ground); the driver cannot tell the two apart. Measure the supply on a second channel if that matters.

docs.text: Repository setup ¶ The one-time steps an org owner runs after creating a repository from the template, and before the first PR. The scripts are in kokeb-labs/.github/org/ . Each one is a dry run unless given --apply ; --org names the organisation (a driver lives in kokeb-labs-drivers , everything else in kokeb-labs ) and --repo limits it to one repository. The rules behind them are in repo-governance.md . 1. Create and scaffold ¶ gh repo create kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-<chip> --private --template kokeb-labs/driver-template --clone cd driver-<chip> git switch -c feat/initial-driver python3 tools/setup.py tools/setup.py asks for the bus and a one-sentence description, scaffolds, builds and runs the host tests; tools/scaffold.py --help lists every option ( --platforms host,esp32 is a driver's default; a library gets host unless esp32 is asked for); it ends with a checklist of what is left to fill in. 2. Apply the org settings ¶ From a checkout of kokeb-labs/.github , after adding the repository to org/repos.json by PR. Its entry sets the About: the description is the README's first sentence ( C++20 driver for the <vendor> <parts> <what it is> (<bus>) ), and the topics are the shared kokeb-labs driver embedded cpp20 misra-cpp header-only plus the bus, the device category, the vendor and the part ( spi eeprom microchip at25040b ): python3 org/kokeb_org.py --org kokeb-labs-drivers --repo driver-<chip> # the plan python3 org/kokeb_org.py --org kokeb-labs-drivers --repo driver-<chip> --apply # settings, Actions, labels, ... A private repository on the free plan gets the settings, Actions policy and labels; security features and rulesets need it public (the tool says which sections it skips). Run it again, with --check to see that nothing is pending, after the repository goes public (section 6). Run it without --apply first to see what changes. 3. Create the labels ¶ --apply in step 2 already creates them; this is the manual way, for a repository outside the org tool. python3 - <<'PY' import subprocess, yaml for label in yaml.safe_load(open(".github/labels.yml")): subprocess.run(["gh", "label", "create", label["name"], "--color", label["color"], "--description", label["description"], "--force"], check=True) PY 4. Require the gate ¶ After the first CI run has produced the check CI gate / gate , add it to the repository's main-review ruleset as described in The required check . 5. Wire it in ¶ Add the repository as a submodule or CMake dependency where it is consumed, in its own pin PR, then follow checklists/new-driver.md . 6. First release candidate and going public ¶ The order that works, and the reason for each step: main green first. Push, and wait for CI on main , including CI gate / gate . The docs publish to gh-pages from main before any tag does. Triage a failure with the release skill, section 5: re-run the failed jobs only when the infrastructure failed. Tag vX.Y.Z-rc.1 on that commit (the release skill). Its CI repeats the run, then the Release workflow publishes the pre-release: firmware, SBOM, checksums. A pre-release publishes its docs under its own tag and takes latest only when no other version holds it. Make it public ( gh repo edit <org>/<repo> --visibility public --accept-visibility-change-consequences ), then python3 org/kokeb_org.py --org kokeb-labs-drivers --repo driver-<chip> --apply : rulesets, secret scanning with push protection, CodeQL and private vulnerability reporting need a public repository. If the last call answers 422, run it again after a few seconds; the new visibility has not reached that endpoint yet. Enable Pages from the gh-pages branch, root, and open https://<org>.github.io/<repo>/ . --check reports 0 change(s) pending . A private repository on the free plan shares a small Actions storage quota with the rest of its organisation. A full quota fails every upload step in every repository of it at once, which looks like a broken workflow and is not one; a public repository does not count against it.

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Every error the driver returns, what it means, and what to measure. Probe the node with a multimeter or a scope first: it should sit between the rails, move slowly with temperature, and be about Rs / (Rs + Rn) of the supply. Error What it means Check InvalidArgument The configuration is not valid Call Validate(config) and look at each field against Configuration : is there a curve? a window for a beta or Steinhart-Hart curve? a wait over 1 000 000 us? both voltages or neither? a delay without DelayUs() ? NotInitialized A read before EnsureInitialized() succeeded Call it first and check its result Bus ReadRaw() or SetBias() returned false The ADC unit, the channel and the pin in your port; the bias GPIO OpenCircuit The node is at the open rail A cut wire or missing part (the node floats to the supply on a low-side divider); a divider that is not powered; a thermistor not soldered ShortCircuit The node is at the short rail A shorted part or wire; a collapsed divider supply on a low-side divider; the wrong channel; the divider side declared the wrong way round BelowRange Colder than the curve or the window, or the resistance is beyond 32 bits The part really is colder; the series resistor or its declared value is wrong; the window is too narrow AboveRange Hotter than the curve or the window, or a resistance of zero The part really is hotter; check the topology; a node at the rail with a margin of 0 Unstable The samples differ by more than max_spread_codes A floating or noisy input; the ADC's source impedance is too high for the divider (add 100 nF, lower Rs ); a switching load on the same rail CodeOutOfScale A sample is at or above 2^ adc_bits The port returns more bits than adc_bits says: fix one of them A reading is plausible but wrong ¶ Symptom Cause Off by a constant The thermistor's own tolerance or the series resistor's: measure R with a meter at a known temperature; set offset_mc or the real series_ohm Off by more at the ends than in the middle A beta curve on a part that is not one: use Steinhart-Hart coefficients or a table ( Conversion ) Too warm, and warmer the more you read Self-heating: lower the supply, raise Rs , or power the divider only while sampling ( SetBias() ) Off by a few percent with a separate ADC reference adc_vref_mv and divider_supply_mv are the real voltages? Reference, range and supplies Moves in the wrong direction topology is the wrong way round Resolution coarse at the ends Normal: one step is worth more where the node nears a rail ( Hardware ) The unit of the number ¶ temperature_mc is milli -degrees Celsius: 25 000 is 25 degrees. docs.text: Worked example: a 10 kOhm chip thermistor ¶ One part end to end, with its numbers: the TDK NTCG163JF103FT1S, a 10 kOhm 0603 chip thermistor, read by a 12-bit ADC. This is the only page that depends on that part's datasheet (TDK, Rev.3, 8 May 2023, one page, p. 1). The table rows are unverified R25, B, the tolerances, the package and the ratings below are from the datasheet. The 39 resistance rows are not : the sheet prints no table and links a separate step file (403 to an automated fetch). The arithmetic (the divider, the interpolation, the step sizes) is computed by the driver and holds for any part with these rows. Datasheet sections this page relies on From TDK none printed Rev.3: Example part: R-T table (rows unverified): Electrical Characteristics, 1degC Step Data link (the table itself is not in the PDF), p. 1 Example part: R25, B and tolerances: Electrical Characteristics: Resistance, B value, p. 1 Example part: package and ratings: Dimension and Construction; Electrical Characteristics: power, dissipation, current, voltage, range, p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The part, as the datasheet gives it ¶ What Value Source R25 10 kOhm, 1 % Datasheet p. 1, Electrical Characteristics B25/85 3435 K, 1 % Datasheet p. 1 B25/50 3380 K, typical Datasheet p. 1 Operating temperature -40 to +150 degrees Celsius Datasheet p. 1 Maximum rated power 125 mW at 25 degrees Celsius Datasheet p. 1 (a secondary listing said 100 mW: wrong) Thermal dissipation constant 1 mW/degC at 25 degrees Celsius Datasheet p. 1 Permissive operating current 0.31 mA at 25 degrees Celsius Datasheet p. 1 Maximum voltage 5 V Datasheet p. 1 Package 0603 (JIS1608): 1.6 x 0.8 x 0.8 mm, grade AEC-Q200 Datasheet p. 1, Dimension and Construction Rows 39, -40 to +150 degrees Celsius every 5 Unverified : not in the sheet; consistent with its B values Thermal time constant not given The sheet lists none The configuration ¶ #include "ntc_thermistor_presets.hpp" constexpr ntc_thermistor :: Config kConfig {. curve = ntc_thermistor :: presets :: kTdkNtcg163jf103ft1s }; The default divider is a 10 kOhm series resistor, low side, ratiometric, on a 12-bit ADC. A table carries its range, so no window is needed. What a reading looks like ¶ Simulated divider, low side, 12 bits (derived from the unverified rows; the host example prints these): True (degC) Resistance (ohm) Code Read (degC) Bound (K) -20 67 800 3570 -20.02 0.26 0 27 280 2997 0.01 0.27 25 10 000 2048 25.00 0.30 60 3 019 950 59.99 0.37 100 975 364 99.99 0.52 145 346 137 144.99 0.88 The bound comes from the declared 1 % on R25 and one ADC step; it grows at the ends because one step is worth more there ( Hardware ). The end rows are reached to within one code: a code that rounds just past -40 or +150 degrees is BelowRange or AboveRange , as it should be. Beta against the table ¶ A beta curve with B25/85 = 3435 K is exact at 25 and 85 degrees and wrong by +3.9 K at -35 and +3.0 K at +145 (the table in Conversion ). That is the reason tables exist: the same driver, the same divider, the same code, a different Curve . What is left to confirm ¶ Download the vendor's 1 degC step file named on the datasheet ( rt_sheets/ntcg163jf103ft1s.csv under the same product folder; it answered 403 to an automated fetch) and compare its 5 degree rows with kTdkNtcg163jf103ft1sRows in inc/ntc_thermistor_presets.hpp . Correct any row in the preset and in the model's copy in tests/mock_ntc_thermistor.hpp : the model's copy is typed separately, so a changed row fails until both agree. Then delete the word "unverified" on the pages that carry it. Check your supply against the sheet's limits (5 V maximum voltage, 0.31 mA permissive current at 25 degrees Celsius): 3.3 V across 10 kOhm and 10 kOhm is 0.165 mA at 25 degrees Celsius. SelfHeatingMicrowatts() gives the power.

docs.text: Download the vendor's 1 degC step file named on the datasheet ( rt_sheets/ntcg163jf103ft1s.csv under the same product folder; it answered 403 to an automated fetch) and compare its 5 degree rows with kTdkNtcg163jf103ft1sRows in inc/ntc_thermistor_presets.hpp . Correct any row in the preset and in the model's copy in tests/mock_ntc_thermistor.hpp : the model's copy is typed separately, so a changed row fails until both agree. Then delete the word "unverified" on the pages that carry it. Check your supply against the sheet's limits (5 V maximum voltage, 0.31 mA permissive current at 25 degrees Celsius): 3.3 V across 10 kOhm and 10 kOhm is 0.165 mA at 25 degrees Celsius. SelfHeatingMicrowatts() gives the power.
